newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Oct 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Oct 10.

text.p: THE DOMINION

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters kept the coalition guessing-game alive yesterday, dropping further hints of support for Labour, but keeping the door open with National. Easing a deal with Labour, Peters created a new definition of "non-negotiable" to remove the potential stumbling block of his commitment to buy back Forestry Corporation. And, he indicated tension between himself and Prime Minister Jim Bolger would not prevent talks between New Zealand First and National after the election.

Labour leader Helen Clark's Cinderella-like transformation on the airwaves has been aided by the fairy-godmother touch of her media trainers Judy Callingham and Brian Edwards. Callingham confirmed she and Edwards had held media-training sessions with Clark over a five-week period. Page 1.

National's election support continues to haemorrhage, according to the latest TV3-CM Research poll, National has only 30 percent of the decided party vote support. With United NZ expected to take Ohariu-Belmont and ACT NZ with 6.4 percent support, that would give the right about 48 seats in the
120-seat Parliament. Page 2.

Health Minister Jenny Shipley and Deputy Prime Minister Don McKinnon are being touted as possible successors to National Party leader Jim Bolger if Bolger fails to secure a governing coalition after Saturday's election. Well-placed party sources said that Bolger was unlikely to retain the leadership if he could not secure a victory. Page 2.

New Zealand First supporters were deserting the party in considerable numbers because of leader Winston Peters' refusal to rule out backing National after the election, Labour leader Helen Clark said. Page 2.
New Zealand heads into uncharted political territory this weekend, according to the influential British magazine The Economist. Page 2.

The number of overseas-owned companies in New Zealand fell by 20 percent in the year to February, according to Statistics New Zealand figures. The percentage of total full-time equivalent employees of overseas-owned firms also fell to nine percent from 16 percent. Page 17.

An election result unfavourable to business would lead to a tragic outcome, Lion Nathan chief executive Douglas Myers said. Myers told an Australian forum the penalties would come "thick and fast" as the world lost interest in New Zealand. Page 17.

Port of Wellington made a full-year profit of $5.3 million after tax, chairman Nigel Gould said. The profit before tax of $7.9 million was a 41 percent improvement on the previous year's result. Page 17.

Market comfort with a Labour election victory was "something of a myth", Bancorp said yesterday. Instead, there were likely to be wild fluctuations and volatility immediately after the election as the markets had a "wake-up call on the realities of who may be playing power broker in the formation of the first MMP-elected government". Bancorp said market reaction had been
distorted by the influx of $5 billion from overseas investors taking advantage of high real-interest rates. Bancorp outlined five possible coalitions and their outcomes on financial markets. Page 19.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

A late burst by ACT NZ leader Richard Prebble in the crucial Wellington Central seat could bring about six of his party's candidates into Parliament. A TVNZ-Colmar Brunton poll last night gave Prebble 30 percent support, up eight points from last month. If Prebble won the seat, ACT NZ would no longer have to
cross the five percent threshold. Even four percent would be translated into five ACT MPs.
Under pressure to declare his hand, New Zealand First leader Winston Peters attempted to send an even stronger message to voters that Labour is his party's preferred coalition partner.

A director of the Reserve Bank Eion Edgar criticised New Zealand First and Alliance economic policy and warned their plans could compromise a Labour-led government. Edgar made his comments on the same day the Prime Minister questioned how far
Labour leader Helen Clark was prepared to shift Labour towards the Alliance to form a government.
A North Shore property sold recently for $4.05 million had been bought from the government two years earlier by CDL Investments for a mere fraction of that price.

A few small shareholders may hold the balance of power between Williams and Kettle and the hold-out minorities in New Zealand Rural Properties. Williams and Kettle's second deadline for acceptance of its cash-and-shares takeover offer for Rural
Properties expires today.

Listed investment company Direct Capital Partners has acquired a 24 percent stake in one of New Zealand's largest information management companies, Gallagher Mailing Services, with a $4 million injection of debt and equity.

The New Zealand dollar finished below US69 cents and the 90-day bank bill yield climbed over 10 percent as rumours about a TV3 election opinion poll swept nervous financial markets yesterday. The rumours, later confirmed, held that the poll
would show a further decline in support for the government.

Broking firms Direct Broking and ANZ Securities have been fined by the stock exchange over a trade in Strada shares at the time of the company's capital reconstruction shortly before delisting in March.

Uncertainty over the outcome of the MMP election has already driven one British-based bond dealer out of the New Zealand market. Zurich Investments, a company dealing in 21 international bond markets, decided at its August meeting the
risk of a post-election regime bringing down the curtain on foreign investment was too high, so it sold all its holdings in New Zealand bonds and currency - a sell-down of around $US70 million.
